findings.title: The longest reading pages have no persistent wayfinding — the only in-page nav sits at the top and scrolls away
findings.detail: Density is genuinely extreme: /type/* measures ~16,860px desktop (~19 screens) and ~27,900px on a phone; /lexicon ~34–35k px; /sides ~7k. Every in-page navigation aid is placed once, at the very top, and is NOT sticky: the type/sides section-nav chips are a plain nav.cluster (Section.tsx:36), the lexicon search + 11 category-filter chips sit above the fold, and the course learn-rail (components.css .learn-rail) has no position:sticky. There is no scroll-spy, no 'back to top', no sticky table of contents. Once a reader is even one screen down a ~19-screen type page, the only persistent chrome is the sticky masthead — whose own page links are hidden behind a hamburger by default (see separate finding). A reader deep in the 'Who you fit' section (which reproduces all sixteen full relation stack-maps) cannot tell where they are or jump elsewhere without scrolling all the way back up. The app already knows how to do sticky sub-navs (the pair page's .persp-bar sticks under the masthead), so the pattern exists — it is just not applied to the pages that need it most.
findings.evidence: type-entp-desktop-light.png (full 16,864px page); crops/type-entp-top.png (chip nav 'The eight seats … Reference' near hero); lex-top.png + lex-mid.png (search+filters at top, none visible mid-page); sides-intp-desktop-light.png; Section.tsx:31-38 (SectionNav = nav.cluster, plain margin, no sticky); src/styles/components.css:659-666 (.learn-rail, no sticky). Page-height figures from session-notes.md.
findings.recommendation: Give the tall reading surfaces (type, sides, lexicon, learn) a sticky in-page nav that docks under the masthead once the top instance scrolls off — reuse the .persp-bar sticky pattern. Add scroll-spy 'on' state so it shows current section, and consider progressive disclosure for the type page's all-sixteen 'Who you fit' block, which is the single biggest contributor to the 19-screen height.

findings.title: On a default signed-in desktop the 12 primary nav tabs are collapsed behind a hamburger — because the chat rail opens itself
findings.detail: The assistant rail defaults to OPEN on desktop (ChatContext.tsx:34-40 returns true when no stored preference and not an overlay). Open, it reserves 384px (--rail), so at a 1440px viewport the masthead container is only ~1008px — below the 1239px container-query threshold that collapses nav.tabs to the ☰ menu (components.css:1036). The result: a first-run user on the most common laptop widths (1440/1536/1600) sees NO horizontal navigation at all — just four icon buttons (?, theme, sign-out, menu) — even though twelve destinations exist (App.tsx:24-37). The tabs only appear if the user closes the assistant or has a viewport past ~1680px. So the app's entire information architecture is one hamburger click away by default, on desktop, which is exactly where a persistent tab bar is expected. This compounds the tall-page wayfinding problem above.
findings.evidence: Every signed-in desktop shot shows only icon buttons, no tabs: home-app-desktop-light.png, type-entp-desktop-light.png, matrix-desktop-light.png, network-desktop-light.png. crops/mast-1680-railopen.png shows the 12 tabs appearing only at 1680px (and even then wrapping). src/chat/ChatContext.tsx:39 (default true); src/App.tsx:24-37 (TABS array, 12 entries); src/styles/components.css:1036-1059.
findings.recommendation: Either default the rail closed on first desktop visit (let the launcher invite it), or keep a compact always-visible primary nav independent of rail state (e.g. a condensed tab set or a persistent left rail) so desktop users are not navigating a 12-destination app through a hamburger.

findings.title: The masthead wraps to two rows in a laptop-width band, breaking the --masthead-h token so deep-link anchors land hidden behind it
findings.detail: tokens.css hard-codes --masthead-h:64px and every scroll offset in the app (.sec scroll-margin, .lex-entry, the sticky .persp-bar 'top') derives from it. The design comment claims the tab row 'collapses to the menu button … BEFORE it would ever need a second line.' It does not: the collapse threshold is 1239px container width, but the twelve tabs need ~1430px to fit on one row, so there is a band where tabs are shown AND wrap to two lines. Measured: at 1300/1400/1500px viewport with the rail closed the masthead is 111px tall, not 64px. Consequence, verified live: navigating to /type/entp#exchange at 1400px lands the target heading at top:80px (its scroll-margin) while the masthead bottom is at 111px — the heading sits 30px BEHIND the sticky masthead. On the pair page the .persp-bar (top:64px, z-30) is likewise overlapped by the taller masthead (z-40). This is a real regression the shots.mjs height-assertion misses because it only checks the collapsed (rail-open 1440) and mobile states.
findings.evidence: crops/mast-closed-1400.png (two-row masthead: 'Lexicon'/'Emoji guide' on row 2); measured mastH=111 at viewports 1300/1400/1500 (mh.mjs); anchor.mjs live result: {mastBottom:111, headingTop:80, hiddenBehind:30} for /type/entp#exchange. src/styles/tokens.css:46; src/styles/components.css:67-72 (nav.tabs flex-wrap:wrap), :162, :495, :952.
findings.recommendation: Raise the tab-collapse container threshold to the width the full tab row actually needs (~1430px) so the masthead is never two rows, OR make --masthead-h dynamic (measure and set as a CSS var). Extend the height-vs-token assertion to cover the 1287–1680px rail-closed band.

findings.title: The gateway-path step labels fail WCAG AA contrast — in both light and dark
findings.detail: The four-step gateway path (GatewayPath.tsx) renders each step's ordinal label ('1 · Ego', '2 · Subconscious', …) as .muted.small text sitting ON tinted step cards (accent-soft lavender / warn-soft tan). Muted ink on a tinted panel drops below AA — axe-core already flags 6 serious color-contrast nodes on '.gpath-step .muted.small' on the type page. The captured crops confirm it visually in light AND dark (the muted labels wash out against the tinted backgrounds), so it is not a light-only artifact. The 'through your Dread' line is also set in --danger, which is borderline on the tan tint in light mode. The palette.test.ts AA assertions pass because they check tokens against the plain canvas, not muted text composited over the soft-tint surfaces.
findings.evidence: crops/type-entp-gpath.png (light) and crops/gpath-dark.png (dark) — '1 · Ego', '2 · Subconscious', '3 · Unconscious', '4 · Superego' low-contrast on tints; same component on sides-intp-desktop-light.png. axe-results.json / session-notes.md: color-contrast serious ×6 on .gpath-step .muted.small. src/styles/components.css:579-600.
findings.recommendation: Darken the step ordinal labels to --ink-2 (or drop the tint behind them), and add these composed muted-on-soft-tint pairs to palette.test.ts so the build guards them the way it guards token-on-canvas pairs.

findings.title: All three typefaces are hotlinked from Google Fonts with no self-hosted fallback
findings.detail: index.html:9-11 loads Newsreader, Inter and IBM Plex Mono directly from fonts.googleapis.com with display=swap; there is no @font-face self-host and no woff2 in the repo. The entire 'reading-first, the canvas is paper' identity rests on Newsreader, yet the app has a hard runtime dependency on a third-party CDN to render it. With display=swap the first paint is always the fallback (Georgia/system/mono) and then reflows when the real faces arrive — a visible FOUT on the load-bearing serif. If Google is slow, blocked (corporate/EU networks, and note this very sandbox), or down, the whole typographic system degrades to Georgia. It also leaks every visitor's IP to Google on each load, a documented GDPR concern. Because wrangler runs every request through the Worker already, self-serving woff2 would be trivial and matches the 'private instrument' posture. (Judged from source per the brief, not from the fallback-rendered screenshots.)
findings.evidence: index.html:9-11 (preconnect + single Google Fonts stylesheet link, display=swap); grep found zero @font-face and zero woff/woff2/ttf assets in src/ or public/. dev-server console ERR_CONNECTION_RESET on the font host confirms the availability failure mode.
findings.recommendation: Self-host the three families as woff2 subsets served by the Worker, declare them with @font-face and font-display:swap, and drop the Google links (keep a system fallback stack, which tokens.css already defines). Removes the FOUT, the CDN dependency, and the privacy leak in one move.

findings.title: Heading levels skip on several pages — visual hierarchy is not carried in the document outline
findings.detail: axe-core reports heading-order violations on the type, calculator and learn pages. Visually the hierarchy reads fine (serif H1, section H2s, sans card-titles), but the DOM outline jumps levels — e.g. card/question labels are styled as headings' visual peers while the real heading sequence skips a level, so a screen-reader or reader-mode user gets a broken table of contents on exactly the tall pages where an outline matters most. Because the app leans on an editorial reading experience, a correct heading spine is also what would power an auto-generated in-page TOC (see the wayfinding finding).
findings.evidence: session-notes.md / axe-results.json: heading-order flagged on type-entp, calculator, learn-stage. Cross-checked visually on calculator-desktop-light.png (numbered questions as h-level peers of section headings) and learn-functions-desktop-light.png. src/components/Section.tsx (h2) vs card-title usage.
findings.recommendation: Audit the heading levels per page so they descend without gaps (h1→h2→h3), demote non-heading labels (card-title, question numbers) to non-heading elements, and then the same outline can drive a generated sticky TOC.

findings.title: The signed-in home centers multi-line body prose, breaking with every other reading surface and the app's own reading-first doctrine
findings.detail: Home.tsx sets textAlign:center on the hero and on several multi-line explanatory blocks ('Everything here is derived. Sixteen wirings produce 256 relationships … Nothing can quietly disagree with anything else.' runs four centered lines; the 'Two things this app insists on' intro likewise). Centered multi-line body copy gives every line a different left start, which measurably slows reading and contradicts base.css's stated 'a size you can actually read' reading-first intent. Every other surface — the marketing home, type, sides, learn, lexicon — left-aligns its prose, so home is the odd one out. A centered one-line hero is defensible; the centered paragraph-length copy is the weak part.
findings.evidence: home-app-desktop-light.png (centered 'Read the wiring.' hero + centered 3–4 line paragraphs); src/views/Home.tsx:38, 41, and the centered section intros at 68/208/211; contrast with left-aligned home-signedout-desktop-light.png and type-entp.
findings.recommendation: Keep the H1 (and perhaps the one-sentence lede) centered as a landing gesture, but left-align the paragraph-length explanatory copy so it matches the rest of the app and reads faster.

findings.title: The floating 'Ask about this' launcher occludes bottom-edge content
findings.detail: When the rail is closed, the .rail-launch pill is fixed at bottom-right on every page (components.css:921-930) with no content padding reserved for it. On mobile it lands on top of real content: it overlaps the last rows of the type page's section-nav chips and covers part of the first lexicon card's diagram. It is the only way back into the assistant, so it must stay visible — but it should not sit on top of tappable/readable content.
findings.evidence: crops/type-mob-top.png ('Ask about this' pill over the 'Who you fit'/'Reference' chip area); crops/lex-mob-top.png (pill over the Ne card's crowd figure). src/styles/components.css:919-930.
findings.recommendation: Reserve bottom padding on scroll containers when the launcher is present (as the calculator already does for its dock via .main:has(.calc-dock)), or inset the launcher clear of interactive content.

findings.title: Masthead icon buttons are 38px — under the 44px comfortable-target size, and they are the whole desktop nav when tabs collapse
findings.detail: .icon-btn is 38×38px (components.css:91-93). That clears the WCAG 2.5.8 AA minimum (24px) but is under the 44px comfortable/AAA target. Normally minor, but per the nav-collapse finding these buttons — including the ☰ that hides the entire primary nav — are frequently the ONLY controls in the masthead on desktop, so their size and spacing (gap --s2 = 8px) carry more weight than usual for a fine-motor or touch user on a hybrid device.
findings.evidence: crops/type-entp-top.png and type-mob-top.png (four 38px icon buttons, tight 8px gaps); src/styles/components.css:89-102, :87.
findings.recommendation: Bump .icon-btn to ~44px (or add padding to the hit area while keeping the 38px visual), especially given the ☰ menu button's outsized navigational role.

findings.title: The matrix's sixteen-relations list is a tall single-column stack, and the grid has an empty corner header
findings.detail: On desktop /matrix, below the 16×16 heatmap the 'sixteen relations' render as sixteen full-width cards stacked in one column (~2000px of scroll) while each card's text only fills the measure — the right half is whitespace, and a 2–3 column grid would roughly halve the section's height and reduce the page's overall length. Separately, axe flags an empty-table-header on the matrix: the top-left corner cell of the grid is a blank <th>, which reads as an unlabeled header to assistive tech and looks like a stray empty box visually.
findings.evidence: matrix-desktop-light.png (Counterpart…Headwind stacked single-column, wide right margin) and matrix-dark equivalent; session-notes.md axe: matrix empty-table-header + dlitem ×6. src/styles/components.css:405-426 (table.matrix).
findings.recommendation: Lay the sixteen relation cards out in a responsive multi-column grid (they already collapse cleanly), and give the matrix's corner cell a visually-hidden label (e.g. 'row type \\ column type').

findings.title: Definition-list-styled rows are marked up as bare dt/dd without a <dl> wrapper
findings.detail: The .row component pairs a dt label with a dd value (components.css:184-205) and is used across type, matrix, calculator, learn — axe counts 84 serious dlitem nodes on a single type page. Visually these are the app's key-value rows ('Relation code   SR · reciprocal SV', the aspect rows, etc.), which look and behave like definition lists but are not wrapped in <dl>, so a screen reader announces orphaned terms/definitions. It is a semantics-behind-the-visual issue: the presentation implies a list structure the markup does not provide.
findings.evidence: session-notes.md / axe-results.json: dlitem serious ×84 (type-entp), ×10 (calculator), ×6 (matrix), ×32 (learn-stage). Visual pattern in pair-entp-infp-desktop-light.png ('Relation code' / 'Camps' rows) and calculator-desktop-light.png. src/styles/components.css:182-205.
findings.recommendation: Wrap each run of .row dt/dd pairs in a <dl> (or switch the rows to non-dl markup with role-appropriate elements); the a11y audit owns the fix but it is the structural twin of the heading-order gap.

notes:
MANDATORY CAVEAT: Google Fonts is blocked by the sandbox, so every screenshot (and my own live Playwright crops) renders fallback faces (Newsreader→Georgia serif, Inter→system sans, IBM Plex Mono→monospace), NOT the real typefaces. I did not critique letterforms or font rendering; all typography comments are about SCALE, alignment and hierarchy only. (The fonts-hotlinked finding is judged from index.html source, not from the fallback screenshots.) Also, full-page screenshots of sticky-masthead pages show the masthead floating mid-image — a capture artifact I ignored.

METHOD: Read the shipped tokens.css/base.css/components.css and DESIGN-SYSTEM.md, opened ~30 screenshots across both viewports and themes, and captured ~15 additional readable crops + live measurements from the real dev Worker (authenticated) to nail down the masthead-height and anchor-offset bugs. Scripts live in scratchpad/crop.mjs, mh.mjs, anchor.mjs, hscroll.mjs; crops in scratchpad/crops/.

STRENGTHS (why the score is high despite 11 findings): Light/dark parity is excellent — every surface I checked (home-app, type gpath, matrix heatmap, network ring, lexicon 34k-px index) converts cleanly to dark with no unconverted white panels, no broken shadows, and function hues re-tuned per theme (palette.ts). Responsive containment is rock-solid: measured zero horizontal document scroll at 390px on matrix/type/lexicon/network/calculator (overflow-x:clip on html + per-container overflow-x:auto). Mobile collapse is thoughtful and correct: masthead → icons+hamburger, section chips wrap, glossary popover becomes a bottom sheet, calculator gets a fixed dock, the rail uses dvh + env(safe-area-inset-bottom) and starts closed as an overlay. The design system is coherent and genuinely encodes meaning (hue=element, size=rank, the 5-property grammar), spacing/measure discipline is consistent, and the breakpoint set is contract-tested. This is a mature, cohesive UI; the weaknesses are concentrated in wayfinding on very tall pages and a few bounded layout/contrast bugs.

REFERENCED, NOT RE-FILED (per brief, owned by other audits): (1) DESIGN-SYSTEM.md documents a brand palette (N #6B3BC4 / S #8A5410 / T #0D6560 / F #AE3355) that ships nowhere — the shipped FN_COLOR is Ne #4C4899 / Se #855723 / Te #326758 / Fe #983E4A; the documented brand hues appear in no rendered surface. Owned by the palette/brand audit. (2) The marketing hero worked-example has ENTP/INFP ease directions swapped vs the engine (P0) — owned by the marketing audit. (3) The systemic axe a11y set (dlitem, heading-order, landmark/region on onramp+calculator) is a11y-audit territory; I cross-checked and filed only the pieces with a direct display consequence (gpath contrast = visual; heading-order and dlitem as hierarchy/structure display-semantics).

DENSITY VERDICT (the headline question): Yes, the tall pages are wayfinding-hostile as shipped — not because the content is wrong but because navigation aids are placed once at the top and never persist, and the sticky masthead's own links are hidden behind a hamburger by default. Type ~16.9k px desktop / ~27.9k px mobile and lexicon ~34–35k px are the acute cases. Fixing finding #1 (sticky in-page nav + scroll-spy) and #2 (don't hide desktop nav) would resolve most of the density pain without cutting content.
scoreRationale: A mature, internally-coherent design system executed with unusual discipline: excellent light/dark parity (no unconverted surfaces on any page I checked), zero horizontal scroll at 390px on the widest pages, thoughtful mobile collapse (bottom-sheet popover, dvh rail, safe-area insets), and a color system that actually encodes meaning. It loses points for a concentrated set of real issues: tall reading pages with no persistent wayfinding (P1), the default-open chat rail hiding the entire desktop nav behind a hamburger (P2), a genuine correctness bug where the masthead wraps to two rows in a laptop-width band and breaks the --masthead-h token so deep-link anchors land hidden (P2, verified live: heading 30px behind a 111px masthead), a WCAG-AA contrast fail on the gateway-path labels in both themes (P2), and fonts hotlinked from Google with no self-host (P2). None are catastrophic and most are bounded, so the work sits solidly in the 'good, with fixable seams' range rather than higher.
strongestThing: Light/dark parity and responsive containment are handled with real rigor: every surface converts cleanly to dark (function hues re-tuned per theme, no orphaned white panels, shadows intact) across pages as long as the 34k-px lexicon index, and there is measured zero horizontal document scroll at 390px on matrix/type/lexicon/network/calculator — the wide artefacts (16×16 matrix, big SVG figures) scroll inside their own overflow containers while html uses overflow-x:clip. Combined with the thoughtful mobile collapse (masthead→icons+hamburger, chips wrap, popover→bottom sheet, dvh + safe-area-inset rail), it reflects a design system that was engineered, contract-tested, and held to its own invariants rather than eyeballed.
